bib.title: Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?", Thibaud Gloaguen, Niels Mündler-Sasahara, Mark Niklas Müller, Veselin Raychev, Martin Vechev (ETH Zurich, LogicStar.ai). Preprint, arXiv:2602.11988v3 [cs.SE], dated 29 Sep 2026 (the printed header says "Preprint"). The title page is the only source for the year. The file name says 2026.

COVERAGE: 69,462 of 69,462 chars read, all 24 pages. That covers the main text, the appendices (A to E), Tables 5 to 8 and the prompts. I skimmed the references. Figures 3, 4, 6 to 8, 12 to 14 and Figure 10 are bar charts. Only their axes were extracted, so no per-bar values come from them except Table 5.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Context files (LLM-generated or developer-written) do not significantly improve task success, while they raise cost by more than 20% on average.
  number: cost +20% (SWE-bench) and +23% (CtxBench) for LLM files; p=0.87 (SWE-bench None vs LLM), p=0.37 (CtxBench None vs LLM), p=0.21 (CtxBench None vs Dev)
  setup: Four agent and model pairs. Claude Code with Sonnet-4.5, Codex with GPT-5.2 and with GPT-5.1 Mini, and Qwen Code with Qwen3-30B-Coder. Benchmarks are SWE-bench Lite (300 tasks, 11 repos) and CtxBench (138 instances, 12 repos). One sample per agent, with temperature 0 (0.7 for Qwen). Significance by Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test.
  quote: "Surprisingly, we find that providing context files does not generally improve task success rates, whileincreasing inference costby over 20% on average."
  where: Abstract, p1; Table 3, p6
- claim: LLM-generated files slightly lower success on average and raise steps and cost.
  number: success -0.5% (SWE-bench) and -2% (CtxBench); +2.45 and +3.92 steps; cost +20% and +23%; drops in 5 of 8 settings
  setup: As above, the four models on both benchmarks.
  quote: "LLM-generated context files cause performance drops in 5 out of 8 settings across SWE-BENCH and CTXBENCH (see Figure 3). Specifically, the average resolution rate is reduced by 0.5%and2%on average on SWE-BENCHand CTXBENCH, respectively."
  where: Section 4.2, p6
- claim: Developer-written files beat LLM-generated ones on CtxBench, and the difference is significant. Their gain over no file is not significant.
  number: +2.4% over None (p=0.21); Dev vs LLM p=0.038; "7% on average" over LLM files; steps +3.34, cost at most +19%
  setup: CtxBench only, 138 instances, repos that commit their own context file.
  quote: "Developer-provided context files improve agent performance by2.4%on average (p= 21%), significantly outperforming LLM-generated ones (p= 3.8%)"
  where: Section 4.2, p6; Intro, p2 ("developer-committedfiles outperformLLM-generatedones by a significant margin of 7% on average")
- claim: Repository overviews do not help the agent find the relevant files faster.
  number: 8 of 12 developer files contain an overview, and 4 of those list the directories; LLM-generated files contain an overview in 100% (Sonnet-4.5), 99% (GPT-5.2), 95% (Qwen3-30B) and 36% (GPT-5.1 Mini) of cases; 3% of instances excluded
  setup: The metric is steps before the agent first touches a file edited in the gold PR patch. The overview judge was GPT-OSS-120B.
  quote: "Both on SWE-BENCHand CTXBENCH, and for all agents, the context files do not meaningfully reduce this metric, while increasing the number of required steps significantly for GPT-5.1MINI"
  where: Section 4.3, p7, Figure 4
- claim: Agents follow instructions in context files, so a lack of instruction-following does not explain the missing gains.
  number: uv used 1.6 times per instance when mentioned vs under 0.01 when not; repo-specific tools 2.5 vs under 0.05
  setup: Trace analysis, with an LLM judge (GPT-OSS-120B) labelling shell commands across all four agents.
  quote: "uvis used 1.6 times per instance on average when mentioned in the context files, compared to fewer than 0.01 times when it is not mentioned, and repository-specific tools are used 2.5 times per instance on average when mentioned, compared to fewer than 0.05 times when they are not mentioned."
  where: Section 4.3, p8
- claim: Context files push agents to run more tests, explore more and use more reasoning, which accounts for the extra cost.
  number: reasoning tokens with LLM files +22% (GPT-5.2) and +10% (GPT-5.1 Mini) on SWE-bench, +14% and +10% on CtxBench; with Dev files +20% (GPT-5.2) and +2% (GPT-5.1 Mini)
  setup: Matched instances. Only the GPT models expose adaptive reasoning.
  quote: "LLM-generated context files increase the average number of reasoning tokens by 22% for GPT-5.2 and 10% for GPT-5.1MINIon SWE-BENCH(respectively 14% and 10% on CTXBENCH), and developer-provided context files increase it by 20% for GPT-5.2 and 2% for GPT-5.1MINI."
  where: Section 4.3, p8, Figure 6
- claim: A stronger model does not write better context files, and the generation prompt makes little difference.
  number: stronger-model files change success by +2% on SWE-bench but -3% on CtxBench
  setup: GPT-5.2+Codex and Sonnet-4.5+Claude Code generate files for GPT-5.1 Mini and Qwen3-30B. The prompt ablation compares the Codex prompt with the Claude Code prompt on all agents.
  quote: "While performance improves on SWE-BENCH(2% on average), it worsens on CTXBENCH(3% on average), showing that stronger models do not necessarily generate superior context files."
  where: Section 4.4, p8
- claim: When all other documentation is removed, LLM-generated files help and beat developer-written ones. The files mostly duplicate existing docs.
  number: +2.7% on average
  setup: CtxBench. They deleted every .md file, the example code and docs/ after generating the file. Excludes Claude Code (cost). Models: GPT-5.2, GPT-5.1 Mini, Qwen3-30B.
  quote: "we find that LLM-generated context files not only consistently improve performance by2.7% on average, but also outperform developer-written ones across settings."
  where: Appendix B, p16, Figure 12
- claim: Removing a section from an LLM-generated file does not significantly change accuracy. Removing the testing section lowers cost significantly (on both benchmarks).
  number: CtxBench accuracy 68.12% full, 66.67% without testing (p=0.80), 62.32% without overview (p=0.15), 63.77% without tooling (p=0.31). Cost $0.4715 full vs $0.3730 without testing (p=0.023). SWE-bench accuracy 54.36% full, 57.72% without testing (p=0.099); cost $0.3272 vs $0.2756 (p=0.0035). Removing tooling lowers SWE-bench cost to $0.2715 (p=0.0012).
  setup: GPT-5.2 only. GPT-5.4 removed each category. McNemar test for accuracy and permutation test for cost.
  quote: "Table 7 shows that the testing category leads to a significant increase in cost in both SWE-BENCHand CTXBENCH, and the tooling category leads to a significant increase in cost for SWE-BENCH."
  where: Appendix B, p17, Table 7
- claim: Context file length does not explain the results, and training-data contamination does not either.
  number: pre-cutoff share of CtxBench instances 17% (Sonnet-4.5), 40% (GPT-5.2), 12% (GPT-5.1 Mini and Qwen3-30B)
  setup: Binned by file length (Figure 13). Split by whether the PR predates each model's knowledge cutoff (Figure 14).
  quote: "Figure 14 shows no significant or consistent difference between pre- and post-cutoff instance success rates, suggesting that contamination does not affect our conclusions."
  where: Appendix B, p17
- claim: Step and cost increases are statistically significant.
  number: permutation-test p-values: SWE-bench steps 0.0287, SWE-bench cost <0.00001, CtxBench cost None vs LLM 0.00064, None vs Human 0.0126
  setup: Stratified permutation tests (Table 6).
  quote: "We find that context files systematically and significantly increase the average number of steps and the cost required to solve instances."
  where: Appendix A.5, p16
- claim: Raw success rates by model (Table 5). The table labels CtxBench as "PLAN-BENCH", an extraction or typesetting slip.
  number: SWE-bench None/LLM: Sonnet 59.9/58.7, GPT-5.2 56.6/54.4, GPT-5.1 Mini 47.7/47.6, Qwen 31.1/32.4. CtxBench None/LLM/Dev: Sonnet 73.2/65.2/70.3, GPT-5.2 65.2/68.1/68.1, Mini 54.3/50.7/55.8, Qwen 45.7/47.1/53.6.
  setup: Success rate in % with standard error (about ±3 to 4.3).
  quote: "None59.9±3.0 56.6±2.9 47.7±3.131.1±2.7"
  where: Table 5, p15
- claim: Cost and step numbers per instance (Table 2).
  number: Sonnet-4.5 SWE-bench cost $1.30 (None) vs $1.51 (LLM); steps 54.4 vs 57.2. GPT-5.2 CtxBench $0.38 (None) vs $0.57 (LLM) vs $0.54 (Dev).
  setup: Mean ± standard error. Qwen cost estimated from OpenRouter prices.
  quote: "None54.4±2.2 1.30±0.07 12.5±0.8 0.32±0.05 40.9±4.2 0.18±0.03 29.7±1.9 0.12±0.01"
  where: Table 2, p6
- claim: Authors' recommendation: omit LLM-generated context files for now. Human-written ones should hold only what the README does not already say (conventions, non-functional requirements) and be evaluated before adoption.
  number: none
  setup: Conclusion drawn from the results above, Python only.
  quote: "We therefore suggest omitting LLM-generated context files for the time being, contrary to agent developers' recommendations, as they don't help improve performance."
  where: Intro, p2
- claim: The CtxBench construction and its scale.
  number: 138 instances from 5694 PRs, 12 repos, at least 400 PRs per repo, 87% of environments kept, 25 of 138 tests hand-edited, mean test coverage 75%, mean context file 641 words and 9.7 sections
  setup: The builder agent was GPT-5.2 with Codex. Repos have a root AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, are Python, and have a test suite. The agent generated the tests and the task descriptions.
  quote: "we obtained 138 instances from a total of 5694 PRs from 12 repositories that meet our criteria, using GPT-5.2 with CODEXas the agent."
  where: Section 3.2, p5; Table 1; App. C
- claim: Developer files differ from LLM-generated ones. They are shorter and score as less AI-written on the Pangram EditLens detector. CtxBench's generated descriptions make tasks easier than SWE-bench, with about 15% higher accuracy.
  number: GPT-5.2 70.8% vs 57.0%; Qwen3-30B 46.9% vs 30.3% (no context files)
  setup: The CtxBench description pipeline applied to SWE-bench Lite.
  quote: "We observe in Table 8 a consistent trend of about 15% higher accuracy, preserving all model rankings"
  where: App. C, p18

LIMITS
- The authors state that the study covers Python only, and that Python is well represented in training data, which may nullify the effect of context files. Other languages and toolchains are untested.
- Only task resolution is measured. Code efficiency and security are not, and the authors name them as open directions.
- They do not show how to generate useful context files. Context-file generation is left to future work, and they cite planning and continual-learning work as possible routes.
- Single sample per agent per instance. The CtxBench sets are small: 138 instances with standard errors of about 4 points, so the differences between None and Dev (2.4%) are within noise (p=0.21).
- CtxBench tests and task descriptions were LLM-generated (GPT-5.2) and partly hand-edited. This makes tasks easier than SWE-bench. The authors say it is "fairer" but this is their own judgement.
- Developer files are not agent-specific and come from niche repos. No Claude Code gain was seen with them (Sonnet-4.5 70.3 vs 73.2 None).
- The file formats tested are AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md placed in the repo root only. Nested files, skills and other mechanisms were not tested.
- The models are dated (Sonnet-4.5, GPT-5.2 and 5.1 Mini, Qwen3-30B), so the results may not hold for newer models.
- The authors' own caveat in App. B: when documentation is missing, context files do help (+2.7%), so the result holds mainly for repos that already have docs.

BUILDS ON: SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024); SWT-Bench (Mündler et al., 2024) for notation; SWE-agent (Yang et al., 2024); SWE-rebench (Badertdinov et al., 2025) and SWE-bench Goes Live (Zhang et al., 2025) for mining new tasks; descriptive studies of context files (Chatlatanagulchai et al., 2025 "Agent READMEs"; Mohsenimofidi et al., 2025); anecdotal reports (Sewell 2025, Sawers 2025); agents.md site and the Anthropic CLAUDE.md guidance; GitHub blog on 2,500 repos (Nigh 2025).

CODE: None worth keeping. The appendix prompts (PR filtering, instance setup, task description template, test generation, trace intent labelling) are in E.1 and E.2, p19 to 24. The task template uses sections Description / Steps to Reproduce / Expected Behavior / Actual Behavior / Specification / Additional Information.

FIGURES (pdf figure captions were not run; the captions below come from the text extraction)
- Fig 1, p2: evaluation pipeline with three settings (Dev file, None, LLM-generated file). Fastest way to see the experimental design.
- Fig 3, p6: success rate by model, per setting, on SWE-bench and CtxBench. The headline result (values are in Table 5).
- Fig 4, p7: steps before the first touch of a patched file. Shows overviews do not speed up navigation.
- Fig 5, p8: increase in tool use (tests, grep, uv, repo tools) with context files.
- Fig 6, p8: reasoning-token change.
- Fig 12, p16: results with documentation removed (LLM files beat Dev files).
- Fig 9: tool calls with and without being mentioned in the file.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The extraction is complete and readable. Bar-chart values are not extracted, only axes. Table 5 labels the CtxBench block "PLAN-BENCH" (a source slip). Some spaces in the extraction are missing, such as "whileincreasing". I did not run the figures script. Page count is 24.
